anatomy.lede: Less than a gram of butterfly, carrying a sun compass, a magnetic compass and a dose of plant poison across a continent.

hotspots.label: Antennae
hotspots.text: The antennae house circadian clocks that time the sun compass, and appear to contain light-sensitive magnetic sensors.

hotspots.label: Compound eye
hotspots.text: Photoreceptors in the topmost row of the eye are arranged to detect the polarisation of skylight, one of the cues the sun compass uses.

hotspots.label: Thorax
hotspots.text: The black, white-spotted thorax holds the flight muscles. Genes for muscle function show the strongest signs of selection linked to migration.

hotspots.label: Orange forewing
hotspots.text: Bright orange is a warning to predators that the butterfly is poisonous. Variation in this colouring is controlled by a single myosin gene.

hotspots.label: Black veins
hotspots.text: Females have thicker black veins than males. Males can also be recognised by a small swollen pouch on each hindwing.

hotspots.label: Spotted border
hotspots.text: Black borders with white spots frame the wings in both sexes.

senses.lede: Getting to a few mountain forests in Mexico from as far away as Canada takes more than one way of finding direction.

senses.name: Sun and polarised light
senses.text: In outdoor flight simulators, turning a polarising filter above migrating monarchs changed their flight direction in a predictable way, showing that the angle of polarised skylight feeds into their sun compass.

senses.name: Magnetic sense
senses.text: An inclination compass, which senses the angle of the Earth's magnetic field rather than its polarity, may guide migrants when the sun is hidden and fine-tune the sun compass on clear days.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: The monarch genome contains monarch-specific expansions of chemoreceptor genes, which may matter for long-distance migration.

body.lede: A monarch is poisonous because its caterpillar eats poisonous plants, and has evolved a body that can tolerate them.

systems.title: Borrowed poison
systems.text: Caterpillars take up cardiac glycosides from the milkweeds they eat and store them, which makes monarchs poisonous to vertebrate predators.

systems.title: A resistant sodium pump
systems.text: Cardiac glycosides attack the sodium pump in animal cells. Monarchs carry three amino-acid changes in this pump; when the same changes were edited into fruit flies, the flies became as insensitive to the toxins as monarchs.

systems.title: Delayed breeding
systems.text: The last generation of the year does not become reproductive. These butterflies migrate and overwinter in reproductive diapause, maturing only in February and March as they head north.

genome.lede: A draft monarch genome was published in 2011: 273 million letters of DNA containing 16,866 protein-coding genes.

findings.title: Clock and compass genes
findings.text: The genome revealed a complete set of molecular parts for the monarch's circadian clock, a vertebrate-like opsin, and microRNAs that differ between summer and migratory butterflies.

findings.title: Born to migrate
findings.text: Sequencing 101 Danaus genomes from around the world showed that the monarch was ancestrally migratory and spread out of North America to its present worldwide range.

findings.title: Efficient flight muscles
findings.text: Migratory monarchs carry a distinctive form of the collagen IV α-1 gene, used in flight muscle, and fly more efficiently than non-migratory populations.

mind.lede: Much of what is known about monarch navigation comes from tethering butterflies in flight simulators and seeing which way they try to fly.

studies.title: Reading the sky
studies.text: Butterflies tested in the morning or the afternoon responded in the same way to a rotated polarising filter, suggesting that polarised light helps them stay on course even under varied skies.

studies.title: A compass for cloudy days
studies.text: In flight-simulator tests, migrants oriented towards the equator using an inclination magnetic compass, but only in ultraviolet-A or blue light between 380 and 420 nm, a detail earlier studies had overlooked.

studies.title: Courtship in two acts
studies.text: Courtship has an aerial phase, in which the male chases, nudges and brings down the female, and a ground phase, in which they mate. Monarchs rely less on chemical signals than their relatives.

survival.lede: Warning colours and stored poison deter most predators, but a few birds have learned to get around them.

tactics.title: Advertised poison
tactics.text: The orange and black pattern warns predators that the butterfly is distasteful, a defence built on toxins carried over from caterpillar to adult.

tactics.title: Safety in the middle
tactics.text: In wintering colonies, monarchs on the edges and in thinned patches of forest are at much greater risk from birds, which may explain why they gather in dense clusters.

threats.title: Bird predation in winter
threats.text: In one 2.25-hectare colony in Mexico, orioles and grosbeaks killed an average of about 15,000 monarchs a day, around 9% of the colony over the winter. They took more males, perhaps because of their fat or because females carry more toxin.

threats.title: Wintering forests
threats.text: The migration itself has been called a threatened phenomenon. In California, introduced eucalyptus trees now hold most wintering sites, standing in for native trees reduced by logging.

life.lede: The monarch goes through complete metamorphosis — egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and adult — several times over in a single summer.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Females lay their eggs on milkweed plants, the caterpillars' only food.

stages.name: Caterpillar
stages.duration: egg and caterpillar together about 2 weeks
stages.text: The caterpillar grows by shedding its skin several times. How fast it develops depends on temperature.

stages.name: Chrysalis
stages.text: The caterpillar stops growing and forms a case around itself. Inside, its body is rebuilt into a butterfly.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Summer adults live a few weeks, mating and laying eggs for the next generation. The late-season generation migrates and can live for as long as nine months.

lifespan.value: 2–5 weeks in summer; up to 9 months for the migratory generation
